growth_story.headline: The Philippines shook off two decades of crises and has grown steadily since 2003; income per person hit a new high in 2025 even as growth slowed.
growth_story.arc: After the debt crisis of the early 1980s, income per person fell 9.7 percent in 1984 and 9.4 percent in 1985, and it did not pass its 1982 level again until 2004. From 1990 to 2002 growth in income per person averaged only 0.6 percent a year, as an earthquake, a volcanic eruption, a long power crisis and then the 1997 Asian financial crisis hit in turn; income per person fell 3.0 percent in 1998. From 2003 to 2025 growth averaged 3.6 percent a year; for the years since 2010 the World Bank credits pro-investment reforms, steadier economic management and a surge in public and private investment. The pace has held: 3.6 percent a year in 2006–2015 and 3.5 percent in 2016–2025, despite a 10.5 percent fall in 2020 during the pandemic. Income per person reached its highest level yet in 2025, though growth eased to 3.6 percent that year as delayed public works and weaker investment held the economy back.

threads.title: Debt crisis, disasters and blackouts
threads.text: The early 1980s debt crisis left a lost decade. The 1990s then brought an earthquake, the Mt. Pinatubo eruption and a power crisis that lasted until 1994, and recovery was cut short by the 1997 Asian financial crisis. Growth in income per person averaged 0.6 percent a year from 1990 to 2002.

since_last_year.text: Growth slowed. Income per person grew 3.6 percent in 2025, its slowest since 2020, as typhoons, floods and governance concerns held up public works and investment fell. The World Bank reports that in 2026 higher energy prices and stalled infrastructure projects slowed the economy further; that year is not yet in the data.

growth_story.tension: The World Bank dates the growth surge to the years after 2010. The data put the break earlier, in 2003: income per person was already growing 4.5 percent in 2004 and 4.7 percent in 2007, and the 2006–2015 average (3.6) is a little higher than the 2016–2025 average (3.5).
